title: The Dancer of the Future: San Francisco to Nice
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: San Francisco: The Sea and the Cracked Fortune (1877-1895)

stops.name: San Francisco, the birth on Taylor Street
stops.campa: Angela Isadora Duncan is born on Taylor Street in San Francisco, the fourth child of the banker Joseph Charles Duncan and Mary Isadora Gray. The city stands at the rim of the continent, salt wind off the Pacific already in the room. Within the year her father's bank fails; scandal and divorce follow hard upon it, and Joseph Duncan is gone from the household almost before the girl can know his face. She will say all her life that she was born by the sea, and that every great event of her life happened again by the sea.
stops.quote: I was born by the sea, and I have noticed that all the great events of my life have taken place by the sea.
suggested_refs: The Isadora Duncan birthplace marker, Taylor Street, San Francisco

stops.name: Oakland, the bank fails, the family scatters into poverty
stops.campa: In October, months after Isadora's birth, her father's bank collapses; the marriage collapses with it and the family crosses the bay to Oakland, genteel poverty replacing the comforts of the Taylor Street house. Mary Duncan gives piano lessons to keep her four children fed; the two boys find odd work on the streets, and Isadora and her elder sister Elizabeth turn to teaching the neighborhood children to dance for pennies, before either girl has been taught herself. No father, no money, no school she can be made to love: only the four of them, and the bay wind, and invention.
suggested_refs: The Duncan family's rented Oakland cottages, moved between through the 1880s

stops.name: San Francisco, Ocean Beach and the rhythm of the waves
stops.campa: On the free afternoons the child walks out to the ocean edge at the far side of the peninsula and stands where the Pacific breaks white on the sand, watching the long rise and fall by the hour. She will say later that this is where the dance begins: not in any studio, not in any book of positions, but in the wave's swell and withdrawal, the tide's push answered by the tide's pull. The city gives her no dancing master worth the name; the sea gives her the first law she will spend a lifetime trying to put back into a human body.
stops.quote: My first idea of movement, of the dance, certainly came from the rhythm of the waves.
suggested_refs: Ocean Beach, San Francisco, seen from the Cliff House promenade

stops.name: Oakland, the First Unitarian Church, first public dance
stops.campa: At thirteen Isadora gives her first public recital in the hall of the First Unitarian Church of Oakland: no ballet slippers, no set positions, only the loose tunic and the bare feet that will become her signature, and the small hired hall standing in for every stage to come. She has already dropped from school more than she has attended it, unable to sit still for arithmetic when the body wants only to move. The neighbors who watch see a strange, grave child; she already believes, and says so to whoever will listen, that she carries a truth about the body that the century has forgotten.
suggested_refs: The First Unitarian Church of Oakland, site of the earliest recitals

stops.name: Oakland, the Delsarte drills, the Stebbins lineage entering her body
stops.campa: By fifteen, grounded already in gymnastics and ballroom, Isadora takes lessons in the system of François Delsarte from a teacher schooled directly in it: Geneviève Stebbins, the American priestess of the notated, expressive body, whose harmonic gymnastics has by now spread out of New York into the whole country. Through this single channel, Delsarte to Mackaye to Stebbins to the fifteen-year-old girl in Oakland, the grammar of gesture, the solar laws of the moving frame, reach her at the root, years before Paris, years before Greece. She has dropped out of school for good; the body is now the only text she studies.
suggested_refs: Stebbins, Delsarte System of Expression (1885), the manual behind the lineage

stops.name: Chicago, the Masonic Roof Garden, 'The California Faun'
stops.campa: Mary Duncan takes her daughter to Chicago with a trunk, some old jewelry, and twenty-five dollars between them. Isadora finds three weeks' work dancing on the Masonic Roof Garden for twenty dollars a week, billed under the name The California Faun: the West-coast wildness sold to the city as novelty. It does not last, and the manager who hired her tries more than management on her; she leaves before the month is out. But a producer named Augustin Daly has seen the strange bare-limbed dancing, and before the year turns he will send for her to come to New York.
suggested_refs: The Masonic Temple roof-garden theatre, State and Randolph, Chicago

segments.name: New York: The Bought Stage and the Broken Mold (1896-1899)

stops.name: New York, Augustin Daly's company, the fairy and the geisha girl
stops.campa: Daly brings Isadora to New York and sets her in his touring company: a fairy in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a pantomime role in Mme. Pygmalion, a quartet girl in The Geisha. It is steady work and it teaches her the machinery of the professional stage, but every night confirms what she already suspects: the pantomime and the drilled ensemble have nothing to do with the thing moving in her. She studies the company's craft with one hand and despises its cage with the other, waiting for the moment she can dance alone, on her own laws, before anyone at all.
suggested_refs: Playbill for The Geisha, Daly's Theatre, New York, 1896

stops.name: New York, leaving Daly, dancing in the drawing rooms
stops.campa: By 1898 she has broken from Daly's company for good and turned instead to the drawing rooms of society hostesses on Fifth Avenue, dancing to Chopin and Schubert for small, expensive, curious audiences in private houses. It is not the stage she dreams of, but it pays, and word begins to travel among the wealthy that a girl in a Greek tunic does something no one else does. She senses already that America will only ever be amused by her, never converted; that the country able to understand what she is doing does not yet exist on this side of the ocean.
stops.quote: America should hear my message. But she is not ready for me yet. I am too far ahead of my time in my own country.
stops.quote_source: Isadora Duncan, attributed, on leaving America (1899)
suggested_refs: A Fifth Avenue drawing room recital, New York, 1898

stops.name: New York, the Windsor Hotel fire, and the cattle boat for England
stops.campa: Their trunks burn in the great Windsor Hotel fire on Fifth Avenue, and out of the ashes Isadora reads a sign: nothing left to lose, nothing to keep her. With her mother, her sister Elizabeth, and her brother Raymond, and hardly any money, she talks a cattle-boat captain into carrying the whole family to England, the four of them signing on under the false name O'Gorman so as not to embarrass the pet of New York's drawing rooms. One morning, with only a few handbags, they go up the gangplank among the pens and the lowing beasts, bound for a continent she has never seen.
suggested_refs: The Windsor Hotel fire, Fifth Avenue, New York, 1899

segments.name: London and Paris: The Vases, Rodin, and Loïe Fuller (1899-1901)

stops.name: London, the British Museum, the Greek vases learned by heart
stops.campa: Landed at Hull and come down to London with almost nothing, Isadora finds her way daily into the British Museum and gives herself for four months to the Greek and Roman rooms: the painted vases, the frieze figures, the bas-reliefs of dancers caught mid-step two and a half thousand years before her. She and Raymond sit for hours before a single krater, trying to see not the pose but the motion the pose has arrested, then rising to test it in their own limbs. Out of this daily study she begins to build the vocabulary of a dance no ballet master ever taught her.
suggested_refs: The Greek and Roman galleries of the British Museum, Bloomsbury

stops.name: London, the drawing rooms of Mrs. Hunter, the first English patrons
stops.campa: As in New York, London's fashionable houses open to her before its theatres do: Mrs. Charles Hunter and other hostesses invite the American girl who dances barefoot in a Greek shift to entertain their garden parties and evening receptions. Painters and poets drift into these rooms and take note of something that will not fit the word 'skirt dancing' the newspapers reach for. The family is still nearly penniless, sleeping some nights in parks when lodging fails, but the introductions compound; each drawing room recommends her to the next, and London begins, slowly, to make her name mean something.
suggested_refs: A London drawing-room recital, 1899, precursor to the Paris debut

stops.name: Paris: the Exposition Universelle, Loïe Fuller, Rodin's pavilion
stops.campa: The family follows Raymond to Paris in time for the great Exposition Universelle, and Isadora walks the fairground from Rodin's private pavilion of plaster and marble to the swirling, electrically lit veils of Loïe Fuller's own theatre, and to the visiting Japanese dancer Sada Yacco. Here, for the first time, she sees on a public stage what she has been groping toward alone: bodies used as instruments of pure sensation, form abandoned for force and light. She settles with her mother and Raymond on the Rue de la Gaîté, in the shadow of the Exposition's last standing wonders.
suggested_refs: The Palais Lumineux and Loïe Fuller's theatre, Exposition Universelle, 1900

stops.name: Paris, Rodin's studio at the Dépôt des Marbres
stops.campa: Rodin, met soon after her arrival, draws her again and again in his cluttered studio among the marble blocks and plaster casts, watching her move as he might watch a model turn under lamplight, hunting the line beneath the pose. He will say of her, to whoever asks, that she may be the greatest woman the world has ever produced; she will say of him that he taught her to distrust the antique copy and go instead straight to nature, the living body, as he goes to it in stone. Between the sculptor's hands and the dancer's limbs a single argument about form passes back and forth.
stops.quote: Sometimes I think she is the greatest woman the world has ever known.
stops.quote_source: Auguste Rodin, on Isadora Duncan, recorded by contemporaries
suggested_refs: Rodin's sketches of Isadora Duncan, Musée Rodin, Paris

stops.name: Paris: the Louvre vases, Raymond's sketchbook, the dances born from images
stops.campa: Raymond spends whole seasons in the Louvre copying every red- and black-figure vessel in its Greek collection, and Isadora dances from the images he draws, passing so quickly from one antique pose to the next that the succession resolves itself, before the eye can separate the poses, into something new: a dance built entirely from held Greek attitudes set moving. She has no teacher now but the museum cases and her brother's pencil. Out of this collaboration comes the first repertory she will call entirely her own: the tunic, the bare foot, the frieze walking.
suggested_refs: The Greek vase collection of the Louvre, studied and sketched by Raymond Duncan

segments.name: Berlin, Budapest, and the Vision of Greece (1902-1903)

stops.name: Berlin, Loïe Fuller's invitation, the touring company
stops.campa: Loïe Fuller comes to Isadora's small Paris studio, watches her dance, and offers to carry her on tour through Germany and Austria-Hungary as part of her own company, underwriting the concerts that will make Isadora's European name. Fuller sees in the younger woman the revival of tragic, Egyptian, Hindu, and Greek rhythm all at once, and says so plainly. The partnership will not survive the year; Isadora's fame outgrows the arrangement almost as soon as it starts, and the two women drift into a coldness neither will ever quite explain, but the tour is the door through which she enters the Continent.
stops.quote: In her I saw the ancient tragic dances revived. I saw the Egyptian, Greek and Hindoo rhythms recalled.
stops.quote_source: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life (1913)
suggested_refs: Loïe Fuller, Fifteen Years of a Dancer's Life, her account of the tour

stops.name: Budapest, the Urania Theatre, the love of Oszkár Beregi
stops.campa: At the Urania Theatre Isadora dances before Budapest and the city answers with the kind of adoration that will follow her the rest of her life: flowers, ovations, a fever of imitation among the young. Among the city's admirers is the National Theatre's leading young actor, Oszkár Beregi, who watches her from the house and writes afterward in his diary of her piercing gaze and her Hungarian passion, though she is not Hungarian at all. The affair that begins this spring is her first great love outside marriage or family, and though it burns out within a few years it leaves Beregi her lifelong friend.
suggested_refs: The Urania National Film Theatre, Budapest, site of the 1902 debut

stops.name: Berlin, 'The Dance of the Future,' the manifesto delivered
stops.campa: Before the Berlin Press Club Isadora delivers the lecture that will be printed as Der Tanz der Zukunft: a declaration that ballet deforms the beautiful body it claims to train, that the dance of the future must rise, natural and unbound, from the solar plexus outward, as the Greeks danced before her. She prophesies a coming dancer more glorious than any woman yet born, the highest intelligence housed in the freest body, and closes by naming the whole enterprise a religious art or nothing at all. It is read as scandal by some and as scripture by the young women already imitating her tunic and her bare feet.
stops.quote: O, she is coming, the dancer of the future: the free spirit, who will inhabit the body of new women; more glorious than any woman that has yet been... the highest intelligence in the freest body!
stops.quote_source: Isadora Duncan, Der Tanz der Zukunft (1903)
suggested_refs: Der Tanz der Zukunft (The Dance of the Future), Berlin, 1903, first edition pamphlet

stops.name: Athens, Kopanos hill, the temple for the clan
stops.campa: The whole family sails to Greece to fulfill a dream long shared: to build, on ground of their own choosing, a house fit for the ancient blood they claim as theirs. They walk every valley of Attica until Raymond finds a hill outside the city whose crown stands level with the Acropolis four kilometers off, Kopanos as the Duncans name it, and there raise stone walls and a flat tiled roof after the manner of Mycenae, meaning it as the seat of a whole clan reborn. Isadora dances barefoot in the Theatre of Dionysus below the Acropolis, believing, for this one autumn, that she has come home to a Greece that never stopped being ancient.
suggested_refs: Kopanos, the Isadora and Raymond Duncan Dance Research Centre, Byronas, Athens

segments.name: Bayreuth, Grunewald, and the Voices from the North (1904-1906)

stops.name: Bayreuth, Cosima Wagner's invitation, the Bacchanale in Tannhäuser
stops.campa: Cosima Wagner, keeper of her husband's festival and its rites, invites Isadora to Bayreuth to dance the Bacchanale in the Venusberg scene of Tannhäuser: the fantasy loosed in the hero's fevered brain, as Wagner himself once described it to Mathilde Wesendonck. Cosima does not approve of the dancer's transparent tunic and sends a long white undershirt to be worn beneath it; Isadora accepts the correction and dances anyway, the first outsider's body ever set loose inside the sacred choreography of the Wagnerian stage. The festival crowd, primed for solemnity, does not know quite what it has seen.
suggested_refs: The Bayreuth Festspielhaus, and the 1904 Tannhäuser Bacchanale staging

stops.name: Berlin, the meeting with Edward Gordon Craig
stops.campa: In Berlin she meets the English stage designer Edward Gordon Craig, son of the actress Ellen Terry, a visionary of bare stages and towering light who recognizes in her the same hunger for a theatre stripped to essence. She will write of the meeting that here stood before her brilliant youth, beauty, genius: a temperament answering her own, the flesh of her flesh, the blood of her blood. They will work and travel together across Germany, Russia, Poland, and Sweden for the next three years, two absolutists of the stage circling each other, neither able to finally submit to the other's vision.
stops.quote: Here stood before me brilliant youth, beauty, genius... In him I had found the flesh of my flesh, the blood of my blood.
suggested_refs: Your Isadora: the letters of Isadora Duncan and Gordon Craig (ed. Steegmuller)

stops.name: Grunewald, the free-dance school opens, six children enter
stops.campa: In the Berlin suburb of Grunewald, Isadora and her sister Elizabeth open a boarding school of free dance, funded entirely out of Isadora's own theatre earnings. In January six little girls enter, Anna, Erika, Irma, Lisa, Margot, and Marie-Theresa, aged four to nearly ten, to be raised inside the system: no barre, no blocked shoe, the natural motion of childhood trained rather than broken. None of them yet know that in fifteen years their surnames will be changed to Duncan, or that they will carry this room's teaching, as the Isadorables, into every hall in Europe and America the mistress herself cannot reach.
suggested_refs: The Grunewald villa, first school of Isadora and Elizabeth Duncan, 1904-1905

stops.name: St. Petersburg, arrival among the funerals of Bloody Sunday
stops.campa: Isadora reaches St. Petersburg within days of the massacre the city will call Bloody Sunday, and her first sight of imperial Russia is a night-long funeral cortège of the dead of the Winter Palace square, coffin after coffin passing under torchlight through streets gone silent with grief and rage. She will say the memory never leaves her, that from this night forward she cannot separate the idea of Russia from the idea of a people made to march behind their own murdered. She dances anyway, within days, before an aristocracy still unaware how little time its world has left.
suggested_refs: Contemporary photographs of the January 1905 funeral processions, St. Petersburg

stops.name: St. Petersburg: Diaghilev, Fokine, Pavlova, and Kschessinska watch her dance
stops.campa: In the same visit the whole constellation of Russian ballet comes to see the American heresy for itself: the critic and impresario Sergei Diaghilev, the choreographer Michel Fokine, the ballerinas Anna Pavlova and Mathilde Kschessinska, the designer Léon Bakst. Kschessinska will write afterward of the enormous impression Isadora's dancing makes on Fokine especially, who at once begins cutting new paths for classical ballet away from the fixed positions he was trained in. Isadora has no idea, dancing in her borrowed tunic before the Maryinsky's own royalty, that she has just handed the coming Ballets Russes half its argument.
suggested_refs: Mathilde Kschessinska, Dancing in Petersburg, her memoir of the Duncan visit

stops.name: Noordwijk, the Netherlands: the birth of Deirdre
stops.campa: On the North Sea coast of the Netherlands, in the seaside town of Noordwijk, Isadora gives birth to a daughter by Gordon Craig, whom she names Deirdre after the tragic heroine of Irish legend. She has refused marriage on principle, as Craig himself refuses it, and the child is born instead into the strange traveling household of the two artists, carried between the German school, the Russian tours, and whatever city holds their work next. Isadora returns to the stage within weeks of the birth, the dance and the motherhood from now on braided together, neither ever fully separable from the other again.
suggested_refs: Deirdre Beatrice Craig, born Noordwijk, 24 September 1906

segments.name: Paris, the Lohengrin, and the Bridge at Neuilly (1907-1913)

stops.name: Paris, meeting Paris Singer, 'Lohengrin'
stops.campa: As the partnership with Craig cools, Isadora meets Paris Eugene Singer, heir to the sewing-machine fortune, at a Paris gathering; she will call him privately by the pet-name Lohengrin, after Wagner's knight who arrives on a swan-drawn boat, for the sheer improbable splendor of his wealth. Singer falls hard and offers what Craig's genius could never afford: money without limit, applied without hesitation to every plan she has ever had for a school, a theatre, a temple to the dance. It is not the love of her life, by her own account, but it is the closest thing to safety she has ever been given.
suggested_refs: Paris Eugene Singer, heir to the Singer Sewing Machine Company

stops.name: Neuilly-sur-Seine, the birth of Patrick
stops.campa: In Neuilly, on the western edge of Paris where the family has settled, Isadora bears a son by Paris Singer and names him Patrick Augustus. Two children now, by two men, neither marriage licensed nor regretted; the household that gathers around them is half nursery, half traveling dance troupe, the Isadorables of the Grunewald school folded into it whenever the school's finances allow. She dances through the pregnancy as she has always danced through everything, and returns to the stage within the year, Patrick and Deirdre carried along on the tours the way other children are carried to school.
suggested_refs: Patrick Augustus Duncan, born Neuilly-sur-Seine, 1 May 1910

stops.name: Meudon: Bellevue, the great school Singer builds her
stops.campa: At Bellevue, on the heights above Meudon overlooking Paris and the river, Paris Singer builds Isadora the vast school-theatre she has always described and never yet possessed: dormitories, a great dance-temple, room for a hundred children to be raised inside her system at once. It is the fullest material form her manifesto has ever taken, money made obedient to a vision Berlin's small Grunewald villa could only sketch. She moves her pupils in, teaches, dreams of the thousand children she will one day train here to carry the free dance into the next century, not yet knowing how little time this house has left as a school.
suggested_refs: Le Pavillon de Bellevue, Meudon, built by Paris Singer for Isadora Duncan

stops.name: Neuilly-sur-Seine, the drowning of Deirdre and Patrick
stops.campa: The car carrying Deirdre, Patrick, and their governess Annie Sim stalls at a taxi crossing the corner by the Neuilly bridge; the chauffeur climbs down to crank the engine, and it lurches forward on its own before he can regain the wheel, crossing the parapet and dropping into the Seine below. Only the driver escapes the water. Isadora, lying on a couch across the city, is woken by a single cry from Paris Singer: the children have been killed. The tears she says have not stopped flowing twelve years later, when she sets the sentence down in her memoir, do not stop that day either.
stops.quote: The tears have flowed for twelve years, since that day... when, lying on another couch, I was suddenly awakened by a great cry: 'The children have been killed.'
stops.quote_source: Isadora Duncan, My Life (1927), introductory chapter
suggested_refs: Newspaper accounts of the accident, 19 April 1913, Neuilly-sur-Seine

segments.name: The War, the Sculptor's Child, and Bellevue Given Away (1914-1920)

stops.name: A borrowed house: the son of Romano Romanelli, born and lost in a day
stops.campa: In her grief for Deirdre and Patrick, Isadora begs a young Italian sculptor and naval officer, Romano Romanelli, met only recently, to give her another child. She bears a son in August; he dies within hours of his birth, and this third bereavement, coming so soon on the first two, so plainly sought as their answer, breaks something in her that will not mend. She drinks more from this year forward, and eats to fill what the drink and the grief hollow out, and the newspapers that once called her divine begin instead to call her ruined.
suggested_refs: Romano Romanelli, Florentine sculptor, father of Duncan's third, unnamed child

stops.name: Meudon, Bellevue given over as a hospital for the wounded
stops.campa: The war empties the school before it can fill it. Isadora gives over the great house at Bellevue to the wounded of the war: first to France's own military hospitals, later, as the fighting drags into its fourth year, to the American Red Cross, which by 1918 is treating gas cases in the very halls she built for dancing children. The pillars and the dance-floor she meant for a thousand pupils hold cots instead; the temple of the free body becomes, without much ceremony, a ward. She does not complain of the exchange; she has already lost more than a house can measure.
suggested_refs: Library of Congress photograph, 'American wounded at Bellevue,' 1918

stops.name: New York, the Metropolitan Opera, the Marseillaise danced in red
stops.campa: On the stage of the Metropolitan Opera House, in the raw grief of the war years, Isadora improvises a dance to the Marseillaise before an American audience not yet certain it wants to cross the ocean and fight. In long Greek robes and a blood-red cloak she moves through the anthem's rising calls, and at the final Aux armes, citoyens! throws the red cloth back over her shoulder, marches to the footlights, and raises her bare arms over the house in open summons. Witnesses report weeping, singing, and applause that will not stop; she has turned her own body into a recruiting poster and does not apologize for it.
suggested_refs: de Lisle, La Marseillaise, as danced by Isadora Duncan, 1917

stops.name: Paris, the calling of the six, the consecration into Duncans
stops.campa: Isadora calls the surviving Grunewald pupils, grown women now, dancing under her name across two continents, to Paris and asks to adopt them outright, a form of consecration, she says, toward carrying on her art in true tradition. No legal adoption is ever completed, but the New York courts change the surnames of Anna, Irma, and Lisa to Duncan for the rest of their lives, and the world will call all six, whether they keep the name or not, the Isadorables. The line that began with six little girls in a Berlin villa in 1905 is formally, if imperfectly, sealed to her own.
suggested_refs: The Isadorables, Anna, Irma, Lisa, Margot, Erika, Maria-Theresa Duncan

segments.name: Moscow, Yesenin, and the Last Fire (1921-1925)

stops.name: Moscow, Lunacharsky's invitation, the school on Prechistenka
stops.campa: Invited by Anatoly Lunacharsky, the new Soviet commissar of enlightenment, Isadora crosses into revolutionary Russia to found a state-supported school of dance for a thousand children of the working poor, the Grunewald dream finally offered the resources of an entire government. She is given a mansion on Prechistenka Street for the work, promised funding the young state can rarely make good on, and throws herself in anyway, teaching hundreds of Moscow's hungry children the same barefoot freedom she once taught six girls in Berlin. Whatever else Russia will cost her, this school, for a few years, is real.
suggested_refs: The Isadora Duncan School of Dance, Prechistenka Street, Moscow

stops.name: Moscow, Yakulov's studio, the meeting with Sergei Yesenin
stops.campa: At a party in the studio of the avant-garde painter Georgy Yakulov, on the poet's own birthday, Isadora is introduced to Sergei Yesenin, the golden-haired peasant lyricist already famous through all of literary Russia. Neither speaks a word of the other's language; it does not slow anything down. He is seventeen years her junior, volatile, already drinking hard, already the country's most beloved living poet, and something between them ignites before the party has ended. She, who has refused every marriage offered her since Craig, will within the year make an exception for him alone.
suggested_refs: Georgy Yakulov's studio, Bolshaya Sadovaya Street, Moscow

stops.name: Moscow, the marriage at the Khamovniki registry office
stops.campa: On the second of May, Isadora and Sergei Yesenin register their marriage at the Khamovniki Civil Registry Office, each taking the other's surname added to their own on the Soviet papers: she becomes, on this one document, Duncan-Yesenina. It is the only marriage of her life, entered at forty-four to a poet of twenty-six who cannot read a line of her memoirs nor she a line of his verse, and both of them seem to consider the mismatch beside the point. He moves into her rooms on Prechistenka; the school and the marriage now share the same roof.
suggested_refs: The marriage certificate, Khamovniki ZAGS, 2 May 1922

stops.name: Boston, Symphony Hall, the red scarf bared to the hall
stops.campa: Detained at the American border on suspicion of carrying Bolshevik contagion in her own person, Isadora arrives in Boston already furious, and at the close of a performance of Marche Slave she seizes the red scarf sewn to her costume, bares her body to the waist before the whole hall, and cries out that this color is her own, the color of life, and that the audience was once wild here too and must not let itself be tamed. Boston's mayor bans her from the city within hours; Washington opens an inquiry into her politics. Within weeks the United States revokes her citizenship, and she never returns.
stops.quote: This is red! So am I! It is the color of life and vigor. You were once wild here. Don't let them tame you.
stops.quote_source: Isadora Duncan, Symphony Hall, Boston, October 1922
suggested_refs: Contemporary press coverage of the Boston Symphony Hall incident, 1922

stops.name: Leningrad, the Hotel Angleterre, the death of Yesenin
stops.campa: The marriage does not survive the tour or the return to Russia; by 1923 Yesenin and Isadora have separated, he sliding deeper into drink and despair, she back to teaching and to grief grown almost habitual. In December 1925 he is found dead in a room of the Hotel Angleterre in Leningrad, having apparently taken his own life after writing his last verses in blood for want of ink. Isadora, already far from Russia by then, receives the news from a continent away; the man she married without a shared language leaves her a widow of a marriage that lasted, in truth, less than a year.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Angleterre, St. Isaac's Square, Leningrad, site of Yesenin's death

stops.name: Viareggio, the seaside retreat with Eleonora Duse
stops.campa: In the aftermath of Yesenin's death Isadora withdraws for some weeks to the Tuscan resort of Viareggio, where the great tragic actress Eleonora Duse, herself worn down by decades of the stage and by her own losses, keeps her company by the sea that Isadora has always claimed as the ground of everything in her. Two women who each remade an art in their own image sit out the Mediterranean winter together, saying little, according to those who saw them, that either would later repeat. She returns to Paris and then to Nice with no money, no company, and no plan beyond finishing the account of her own life.
suggested_refs: Viareggio, Tuscany, winter retreat of Duncan and Eleonora Duse, 1926

stops.name: Nice, the rented studio, dictating My Life
stops.campa: Living now in a rented studio on the Riviera, out of money, going to parties chiefly to eat the food laid out for other guests, Isadora signs a contract with the Liveright publishing house of New York and spends six months dictating her memoirs, usually after a drink or several, to whatever secretary can keep pace with her. The manuscript she calls My Life ends deliberately with her departure for Russia in 1921, the later grief and the failed marriage left for another book she will not live to write. She sends the finished typescript to New York in the late summer, still dancing when anyone will pay to watch her.
suggested_refs: My Life (Liveright, 1927), first edition, published weeks after her death

stops.name: Nice, the Promenade des Anglais, the scarf, the little Amilcar
stops.campa: On the evening of the fourteenth of September Isadora climbs into a small open Amilcar driven by a young mechanic, Benoît Falchetto, wearing a long hand-painted silk scarf, a gift from her friend Mary Desti. As the car pulls away she calls back to the friends on the pavement: Adieu, mes amis, je vais à la gloire, farewell, I go to glory, though one witness later insists the words were je vais à l'amour. Before the car has gone a hundred yards the scarf catches in the spokes of the rear wheel; she is thrown from the seat, her neck broken, dead in an instant on the Promenade she loved.
stops.quote: Adieu, mes amis. Je vais à la gloire!
stops.quote_source: Isadora Duncan, last words, Nice, 14 September 1927 (reported by Mary Desti)

stops.name: Paris, Père Lachaise, the ashes laid beside her children
stops.campa: Her body is brought back to Paris and cremated; the ashes are placed in the columbarium of Père Lachaise, close by the urns of Deirdre and Patrick, the two children the Seine took from her fourteen years before. My Life appears in New York within weeks, the book she finished only just in time, already speaking of her in the past tense to a public still absorbing the manner of her death. The dance she founded on no fixed step and no written notation survives her the only way she ever said it could: carried on in other bodies, the Isadorables and their pupils' pupils, rather than fixed on any page.
suggested_refs: The columbarium of Père Lachaise Cemetery, Paris, resting place of Isadora Duncan
